summary: This standards-track memo defines a set of SNMP managed objects for monitoring and managing DOCSIS-compliant cable modems and cable modem termination systems. It replaces RFC 2669. It was itself later updated by RFC 9141.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 4639 is a list of the counters and settings that a network manager can read and change on a cable modem or on the equipment at the head end. It follows the usual SNMP model: each item has a name, a type and an access level.

The document also explains how the pieces fit together, in particular the order in which a cable modem applies its filters to a packet, and it lists which settings are safe to change and which are not.

subtitle: The SNMP objects a network manager uses to see and control cable modems and head-end equipment.

tldr.problem: A cable network operator has to manage thousands of cable modems spread over a metropolitan area, plus the equipment at the head end. Without a shared set of objects, every vendor's equipment would need its own management scheme and the operator's tools could not talk to all of it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4639 defines a MIB module, a named set of SNMP objects, grouped into seven components that cover the device itself, software upgrades, provisioning servers, events, filters and customer premises devices. It also defines the order in which the filters are applied to traffic.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from December 2006 that obsoletes RFC 2669, and it has since been updated by RFC 9141. It warns that improper manipulation of the objects could deny service to many users, and it recommends SNMPv3 rather than the older versions.

today: RFC 4639 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2006. It obsoleted RFC 2669, and it has since been updated by RFC 9141. The MIB module it defines is still the one registered under the identifier docsDevMIB.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base, or MIB. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol. Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms defined in the Structure of Management Information, and this memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to SMIv2, as described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

This MIB module provides a set of objects required for the management of DOCSIS-compliant cable modems and cable modem termination systems. The specification is derived from the DOCSIS Radio Frequency Interface specification. The DOCSIS 1.0 standard only required that cable modems implement SNMPv1 and process IPv4 customer traffic, and design choices in the original version of this MIB module reflected those requirements. DOCSIS 1.1 and DOCSIS 2.0 require support for SNMPv3 as well as SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c, and the changes in this MIB module over the previous proposed standard version reflect those additional requirements.

Future versions of DOCSIS, starting with DOCSIS 3.0, are expected to require support for IPv6 both as a customer premises equipment protocol and as one supported by the network elements of the system. The compliance statements in this version of the MIB module require support only for IPv4 addresses, because the current versions of the DOCSIS protocols, 1.0, 1.1 and 2.0, are not IPv6 capable. Although support for IPv6 will require changes to the DOCSIS protocols, it is expected that the only changes needed to the MIB module itself will be the addition of new compliance statements that mandate support for IPv6 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is the shared vocabulary a network manager uses to ask a device what it is doing and to tell it what to do. This document defines the vocabulary for cable equipment.

sections.title: Cable Network Terms
sections.content:
The terms in the document are derived either from normal cable system usage or from the documents associated with the DOCSIS process.

CATV originally meant Community Antenna Television and is now used to refer to any cable or hybrid fiber and cable system used to deliver video signals to a community. A CM, or cable modem, acts as a slave station in a DOCSIS-compliant cable data system. A CMTS, or cable modem termination system, is a generic term covering a cable bridge or cable router in a head-end; it acts as the master station in a DOCSIS-compliant cable data system, it is the only station that transmits downstream, and it controls the scheduling of upstream transmissions by its associated cable modems.

DOCSIS means Data-Over-Cable Service Interface Specification, a term referring to the ITU-T Recommendation J.112 Annex B standard for cable modem systems. Downstream is the direction from the head-end towards the subscriber, and upstream is the direction from the subscriber towards the head-end. The head-end is the origination point in most cable systems of the subscriber video signals, and is generally also the location of the termination system equipment. A MAC packet is a DOCSIS packet data unit. RF means radio frequency.

SNMP is the protocol used for network access to MIB objects, and the three most commonly used versions are SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3.
sections.plainLanguage: A cable network has one master and many slaves. The master is the termination system at the head end; the slaves are the cable modems in subscribers' homes. Traffic downstream goes from the master to the modems, and upstream comes back the other way, with the master deciding when each modem may speak.

sections.title: The Seven Groups of the MIB
sections.content:
The MIB module is structured into seven components. A component contains one or more MIB groups related by deprecation or logical extension.

The docsDevBaseGroup extends the MIB-II system group of RFC 3418 with objects needed for cable device system management. Related to it are the docsDevBaseIgmpGroup, which enables IGMP status and control, and the docsDevBaseMaxCpeGroup, which manages the maximum number of customer premises devices permitted access through the cable modem.

The docsDevNmAccessGroup and the docsDevNmAccessExtGroup provide a minimum level of SNMP access security. With the completion of the SNMP coexistence document, RFC 3584, these groups have been deprecated in this version of the MIB.

The docsDevSoftwareGroup, updated by the docsDevSoftwareGroupV2, provides information for network-downloadable software upgrades. The docsDevServerGroup, updated by the docsDevServerGroupV2, provides information about the progress of the interaction between the device and various provisioning servers. The docsDevEventGroup, updated by the docsDevEventGroupV2, provides control and logging for event reporting; with the addition of the SNMP Notification MIB, RFC 3413, and the Notification Log MIB, RFC 3014, the objects in this module have been modified to allow for their use.

The docsDevFilterGroup configures filters at the link layer and IP layer for bridged data traffic. This group has been deprecated in this version of the MIB in favour of the docsDevFilterLLCGroup and by groups from the Differentiated Services MIB, specifically the groups representing the Data Path, Classifier and Actions tables.

The docsDevCpeGroup, updated by the docsDevInetCpeGroup, provides control over which IP addresses may be used by customer premises devices, such as PCs, serviced by a given cable modem. This provides anti-spoofing control at the point of origin for a large cable modem system. This group is separate from docsDevFilter, primarily because it is only implemented on the cable modem and must not be implemented on the termination system.

The MIB module imports definitions normatively from INET-ADDRESS-MIB, SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB, IF-MIB, RMON2-MIB and DIFFSERV-MIB, and includes DESCRIPTION and REFERENCE clauses that normatively refer to RFC 868, RFC 3617 and the DOCSIS specifications.

Most of the tables in the module are specified not to let objects persist across reboots. The expectation and current operational practice is that on reboot these tables are cleared and repopulated from the DOCSIS configuration file supplied by the cable operator, which enables a cable modem to adapt to the current operator's environment and in turn enables portability across different operators. A notable exception is the event table, since it is useful to maintain a record of events across reboots for debugging purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: The module is split into seven groups, and some of them have already been superseded by better mechanisms elsewhere. The filter group, for instance, has been replaced by the standard Differentiated Services tables so that IPv6 filtering and traffic marking work.

sections.title: Software Upgrades, Events and Throttling
sections.content:
The cable modem software upgrade process is documented in the DOCSIS Radio Frequency Interface specification. From a network management station, the operator sets the software server object to the address of the Trivial File Transfer Protocol server for software upgrades, sets the software filename object to the file pathname of the software upgrade image, and sets the software administrative status object to upgrade-from-mgt.

Although DOCSIS only specifies the implementation of TFTP for file transfers, other functional entities embedded within the cable device, particularly a PacketCable Multimedia Terminal Adapter, specify the optional implementation of HTTP for file transfers. The value of the transport protocol object determines which protocol is used for an SNMP-initiated software upgrade. One reason for the SNMP-initiated upgrade is to allow loading of a temporary software image, such as special diagnostic software, that differs from the software normally used on that device without changing the provisioning database.

Software upgrades should not be accepted blindly by the cable device. The device may refuse an upgrade if the download is incomplete, if the file contents are incomplete or damaged, or if the software is not intended for that hardware device, which may include the case of a feature set that has not been purchased. A cable device that implements the code verification mechanisms of Baseline Privacy Plus verifies the source and integrity of the downloaded image by validating one or more code verification signatures bundled within the software upgrade.

The module provides control facilities for reporting events through syslog, notifications, and non-volatile logging. Additional controls allow the agent to use the SNMP Notification MIB and the Notification Log MIB for event notification. The conventions for event reporting are outside the scope of the document.

The cable modem and termination system must provide support for notification message throttling, and the network operator can use notification rate throttling or notification limiting by manipulating the appropriate MIB variables. In the first rate control method, the device ceases to send notifications when the rate exceeds the specified maximum message rate, and resumes only if reactivated by a network management station request. In the second method, the device resumes sending notifications when the rate falls below the specified maximum message rate. The operator configures the maximum message rate by setting the measurement interval in seconds and the maximum number of notifications to be transmitted within that interval, and can query both the operational throttling state and the administrative throttling state.

Notification limiting is the other option: the device ceases to send notifications when the number of notifications exceeds the specified threshold, and resumes only when the measurement interval has passed. For this case the operator defines the maximum number of notifications he is willing to handle and sets the measurement interval to a large number, in hundredths of a second, and the administrative throttling state is set to stop at that threshold.
sections.plainLanguage: Two jobs here. The first is telling a modem to fetch new software from a server, with an object that chooses whether the transfer uses TFTP or HTTP. The second is stopping a flood: a modem can be told to stop sending notifications above a rate, and to start again when the rate falls or the interval passes.

sections.title: The Filter Chain
sections.content:
The module provides objects for both Link Layer Control and IP protocol filters. The link layer filter entries can be used to limit forwarding to a restricted set of network-layer protocols, such as IP, IPX, NetBIOS and Appletalk. The IP protocol filter entries can be used to restrict upstream or downstream traffic according to source and destination IP addresses, transport-layer protocols such as TCP, UDP and ICMP, and source and destination TCP or UDP port numbers.

In general, a cable modem applies filters, or more properly classifiers, in an order appropriate to the layering model. The inbound MAC or link layer filters are applied first, then the special filters, then the IP layer inbound filters, then the IP layer outbound filters, and then any final link layer outbound filters.

The inbound link layer filters are contained in the link layer filter table and are applied to level-2 frames entering the cable modem from either the radio frequency MAC interface or from one of the customer premises equipment interfaces. These filters prohibit the processing and forwarding of certain types of level-2 traffic that may be disruptive to the network. They can be set to cause the modem either to drop frames that match at least one filter, or to process a frame that matches at least one filter. Example configurations would be to permit only IP and ARP traffic, or to drop NetBIOS traffic.

Special filters are applied after the packet is accepted from the MAC layer by the IP module, but before any other processing is done. They apply only to a very specific class of traffic. The IP spoofing filters are applied to packets entering the modem from one of the customer premises interfaces and are intended to prevent a subscriber from stealing or misusing IP addresses that were not assigned to them. If the filters are active, the source address of the IP packet must match at least one IP address in one of the two spoofing tables, or it is discarded without further processing. The device consults the IPv4 spoofing table before the IPv6 one, to prevent implementation ambiguity. The tables can be populated automatically, using the first N different IP addresses seen from the customer side, and the policy for doing that is controlled by the enrolment and maximum device objects as well as by the management agent.

The SNMP access filters are applied to SNMP packets entering from any interface and destined for the cable modem. If the packets enter from a customer premises interface, the SNMP filters are applied after the IP spoofing filters. The filters only apply to SNMPv1 or SNMPv2c traffic and are not consulted for SNMPv3 traffic, whose access control is specified in the User Security Model MIB.

The IP filtering table acts as a classifier table. Each row describes a template against which IP packets are compared, including source and destination addresses and their masks, upper level protocol, source and destination port ranges, and Terms of Service values, together with interface and traffic direction match values that have to be considered in combination. All columns of a particular row must match for the packet to match the row.

When classifying a packet, each table is scanned beginning with the lowest numbered filter. If the agent finds a match, it applies the group of policies specified. If the matched filter has the continue bit set, the agent continues the scan and may match additional filters and apply additional policies. Once a packet is matched, one of three actions happens according to the control setting in the row: the packet may be dropped, in which case no further processing is required; it may be accepted and processing continues; or it may have a set of policy actions applied to it. The IP filtering table and related tables have been deprecated in this version of the MIB in favour of the Data Path, Classifier and Action tables from the Differentiated Services MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet is checked in a fixed order: first the link layer filters, then the special filters for spoofing and SNMP access, then the inbound IP filters, then the outbound ones, and finally the outbound link layer filters.

sections.title: What Changed Since RFC 2669
sections.content:
This version of the MIB module was published as RFC 4639, and its revision description lists the modifications made since RFC 2669.

The docsDevFilter group was deprecated in favour of the DiffServ MIB groups, to enable support for IPv6 filtering and DiffServ Code Point marking. The docsDevCpeGroup was deprecated in favour of the docsDevCpeInetGroup, to enable support of IPv6, and various InetAddress objects were added to enable IPv6 support. The docsDevNmAccessTable was deprecated in favour of SNMP coexistence and SNMPv3, yet docsDevNmAccessTrapVersion was added and docsDevNmAccessIp was clarified for current use of the table.

Several new objects were added. docsDevIgmpModeControl was added for management and control of the IGMP mode of operation, and docsDevMaxCpe was added for management of the maximum number of customer premises devices permitted access through a cable modem. docsDevSwServerTransportProtocol was added, with modifications to the software object descriptions, to enable software downloads via either TFTP or HTTP.

On the event side, docsDevEvThrottleInhibited was replaced with docsDevEvThrottleThresholdExceeded to simplify event threshold management, and docsDevEvReporting was modified to enable local logging to the internal volatile log and not to the internal non-volatile log. The compliance statement was modified to make the docsDevCpe objects optional, and placeholders were created for two object identifiers in the policy table that were never used. The document also lists many smaller corrections, including added units clauses, a reference to a configuration server object, clarified scoping of notifications, defined enumerated types for the event level and priority objects, and clarified non-persistence across reboots for all tables.
sections.plainLanguage: The big changes are about IPv6 and about SNMPv3. The old filter tables and the old access table were retired, and the objects that replaced them work with both address families.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This MIB module relates to a system that will provide metropolitan public internet access. Improper manipulation of the objects it represents may result in denial of service to a large number of end users. Manipulation of the network management access table, the filter tables, and the elements of the customer premises device groups may allow an end user to increase their service levels, spoof their IP addresses, change the permitted management stations, or affect other end users in either a positive or negative manner.

It is recommended that implementers prevent the tiny fragment and overlapping fragment attacks for the IP filtering tables, as discussed in RFC 1858 and RFC 3128. Prevention of these attacks can be implemented with three rules when TCP source or destination port filtering is enabled: admit all packets with fragment offset greater than or equal to 2; discard all packets with fragment offset equal to 1, or with fragment offset equal to 0 and fragment payload length less than 16; and apply filtering rules to all packets with fragment offset equal to 0.

The module does not affect confidentiality of services on a cable modem system, since Baseline Privacy and Baseline Privacy Plus specify the implementation of the DOCSIS mechanisms for data transmission confidentiality.

A number of management objects have a read-write or read-create access clause and may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The use of the network management access table to specify management stations is considered only limited protection and does not protect against attacks that spoof the management station's IP address; stronger mechanisms such as SNMPv3 security should be considered where possible, and SNMPv3 USM and VACM must be used with any v3 agent that implements this module. The modem may have its software changed by the management system, and an improper software download may result in substantial vulnerabilities and the loss of the ability of the management system to control the modem, so a cable device should implement the code verification mechanisms of Baseline Privacy Plus. The device may be reset by setting the reset object to true, which reloads its configuration files and eliminates all previous non-persistent network management settings, and so may provide a vector for attacking the system.

Setting the event throttle administrative status to unconstrained, which is also the default, may cause flooding of traps that can disrupt network service. Setting the filter default actions may cause significant changes to default traffic filtering. Setting the customer premises enrolment object to any may cause the spoofing table to be populated, which may not be the intended functionality. Some readable objects are also sensitive: rows from the network management access table may give an attacker enough information to spoof management stations, the current software version object may give hints about known vulnerabilities, and the filter tables may give clues for attacking the device and other subscriber devices.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is no control over who on that network is allowed to read or change the objects in this module. It is recommended that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: These objects control who gets service, who may spoof which address, and what software a device runs. A management station that can write them can therefore do a lot of damage, which is why the document pushes SNMPv3 rather than the older versions.

viz.caption: The seven components of the MIB module

items.title: docsDevBaseGroup
items.text: Extends the MIB-II system group with the objects needed for cable device system management. Related groups cover IGMP status and control and the maximum number of customer premises devices.

items.title: docsDevNmAccessGroup
items.text: Provides a minimum level of SNMP access security. Deprecated in this version in favour of SNMP coexistence and SNMPv3.

items.title: docsDevSoftwareGroup
items.text: Provides information for network-downloadable software upgrades.

items.title: docsDevServerGroup
items.text: Provides information about the progress of the interaction between the device and the various provisioning servers.

items.title: docsDevEventGroup
items.text: Provides control and logging for event reporting through syslog, notifications and non-volatile logging.

items.title: docsDevFilterGroup
items.text: Configures filters at the link layer and IP layer for bridged data traffic. Deprecated in favour of the link layer control group and the Differentiated Services MIB groups.

items.title: docsDevCpeGroup
items.text: Controls which IP addresses may be used by customer premises devices. Implemented on the cable modem only, not on the termination system.

viz.caption: What an IP filter can do with a matching packet

items.label: Drop the packet
items.desc: All packets matching the filter are discarded and scanning of the rest of the filter list is aborted. This is the default.

items.label: Accept the packet
items.desc: Matching packets are accepted for further processing, such as bridging.

items.label: Apply a policy
items.desc: The policy entries matched by the policy identifier in the policy table are executed.

items.title: One object, many users
items.text: This module runs on equipment providing metropolitan public internet access, so improper manipulation may deny service to a large number of end users.

items.title: Service levels can be raised
items.text: Writing to the access and filter tables may let a subscriber increase their service levels, spoof their addresses, or change the permitted management stations.

items.title: Software can be replaced
items.text: The software upgrade objects let a management station replace the software on a device, so an improper download could leave it unmanageable.

items.title: A reset is an attack
items.text: Setting the reset object to true reloads the configuration and clears all non-persistent settings, which is a vector for attacking the system.

items.title: Reads can leak too
items.text: The access table rows, the current software version and the filter tables can give an attacker what they need to spoof a management station or find a way in.
